title: Place Value Board
context: Grade 5, the pages on place value in decimals. An adult sees the familiar chart with three columns added. What the pages are doing is carrying the chart on past the ones, so each place after the point is worth a tenth of the place before it. The key names a place where a place value is asked; here a place value is always an amount, and which place is asked separately.

writeup.why: Place a decimal on a place value chart, give each digit's place value as an amount, compare the values of one digit in two places, and change a decimal by an amount in one place.
writeup.look: A place value chart of six columns with the point fixed after the Ones, a tray of digit tiles under it, and the Which place and Worth cards beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Place Value Board' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many tiles are on the chart. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The chart spans the working area from x 110 to x 1030 at y 230, six columns of one width, 140 across, headed Hundreds, Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths, with a narrow column 40 across for the large near-black point between Ones and Tenths. Tiles are 110 across and snap to the middle of their column at y 330, deep blue. An empty place inside the number holds a grey 0 labelled Place holder. The tray of tiles runs along y 640. The Which place card sits at x 110, y 470 and the Worth card beside it at x 420, the worth written three ways, a count, a fraction and a decimal. On the third phase the Two places panel sits at x 760, y 470, its two worths one above the other with their points in one line and the difference in green under a ruled line. On the last phase each nudge arrow stands above its column head at y 200. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key, a fraction bar key and a word pad of place names, for setting a decimal, or for typing a place or a place value into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last decimal on the chart with one tile's place named above it and its worth written under it.

source_tool.description: A place value chart runs across the working area, six columns of one width headed Hundreds, Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths, with a narrow column for the large near-black point fixed between Ones and Tenths. Digit tiles wait in a tray under the chart; dragged into a column, a tile snaps to it, deep blue for the decimal the question gives. A tap on a tile asks two things in turn: first the column head lights amber and the Which place card names the place, then the Worth card under the tile shows its place value three ways, as a count of that place, as a fraction and as a decimal. An empty place inside the number holds a grey 0 labelled Place holder. On the third phase, when one digit stands in two columns, a Two places panel beside the chart sets their two worths one above the other and subtracts them, with the difference in green. On the last phase a nudge arrow over each column adds or takes away one of that place, only that column's tile changes, and the new decimal is written in green under the chart. A number pad sets any decimal with up to three places and up to three digits before the point. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many tiles are on the chart.
source_tool.art_direction: A place value chart, chalked on the floor / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.

voice.opening: A place value chart, with room past the point.
voice.onFinish: Every digit has a place, and a worth that goes with it.

phase_map.concept: The chart goes past the point
The place value of a digit

placement.where: After the class has stood in columns chalked on the floor, one digit card each, with the dot card between Ones and Tenths. The tool is what asks which place and what it is worth as two questions, and what changes one column while the others stay still.

answer_key.rule: The places to the right of the point are tenths, hundredths and thousandths. Which place a digit is in is a name, such as the hundredths place. Its place value is what it is worth, an amount, such as 4 hundredths, 4/100 or 0.04. The same digit is worth ten times as much one place to the left. The difference of the place values of one digit in two places is found by subtracting the smaller worth from the greater. Adding an amount in one place changes that place's digit, unless it runs past nine.
answer_key.wrong: The chart is shown again with the tile's column head lit and its worth written three ways under it, and the child's answer set beside the Worth card, so the child sees whether it named a place or gave an amount. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The digits before the point go in the tens and ones columns: 6 tens and 3 ones.
The point sits after the ones.
After the point come tenths, hundredths and thousandths: 5, 0 and 8.
The 0 holds the hundredths place open.
items.answer: 6 tens, 3 ones, 5 tenths, 0 hundredths and 8 thousandths
items.question: Put 63.508 on the place value chart. Which digit is in each place?
items.checkpoint: After the point come tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
items.misconception: Putting the 8 in the hundredths column and leaving out the 0, which turns eight thousandths into eight hundredths.

steps: Count the places after the point: 2 is in the tenths place, 8 in the hundredths place.
So the 8 sits in the hundredths place.
Written as a fraction that is 8/100, and as a decimal 0.08.
items.answer: The hundredths place. Its place value is 8 hundredths, which is 8/100 or 0.08
items.question: In 4.286, which place is the 8 in, and what is its place value?
items.checkpoint: The place tells where a digit sits, and the place value tells how much it is worth.
items.misconception: Answering hundredths alone, which names the place but not the amount the 8 is worth.

steps: The first 5 is in the ones place, so it is worth 5.
The second 5 is in the hundredths place, so it is worth 5 hundredths, 0.05.
Subtract the smaller worth from the greater, with the points in one line: 5.00 - 0.05 = 4.95.
items.question: In 5.45, what is the difference between the place values of the two 5s?
items.checkpoint: One digit is worth different amounts in different places.
items.misconception: Answering 0, because the two digits are both 5, though they sit in different places.

steps: The other digits stay as they are, so the number is 2.391.
items.question: What number is 4 hundredths greater than 2.351?
items.checkpoint: Adding an amount in one place changes that place's digit.
items.misconception: Adding 4 to the thousandths digit and writing 2.355, which is 4 thousandths greater, not 4 hundredths.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.

items.question: Put 7.24 on the place value chart. Which digit is in the tenths place?
What is the place value of 6 in 0.461?
In 15.093, which place is the 9 in?
What is the place value of 3 in 12.803?
In 2.62, what is the difference between the place values of the two 2s?
items.final_answer: 1.98. The first 2 is worth 2 and the second is worth 0.02, and 2.00 - 0.02 = 1.98

items.question: What number is 3 tenths greater than 5.26?
items.final_answer: 5.56. Only the tenths digit changes, from 2 to 5

items.question: In 44.4 the digit 4 appears three times. What is each 4 worth?
What number is 2 hundredths less than 6.145?
items.final_answer: 6.125. Only the hundredths digit changes, from 4 to 2

teaching_notes: Extend the chart the class already knows: the ones stay where they are and the point is drawn after them. Ask which place a digit is in, then ask what it is worth; those are two different questions with two different answers. Give a place value as an amount, such as 4 thousandths, 4/1000 or 0.004, and accept any of the three. The same digit is worth ten times as much one place to the left. When one place changes, only its digit changes, unless it runs past nine.
generation_prompt: Build a decimal place value tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A chart of six columns of one width runs across the working area, headed Hundreds, Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths, with a narrow column holding a large near-black point between Ones and Tenths. Digit tiles in a tray under the chart drag into the columns and snap, deep blue. A tap on a tile first lights its column head amber and fills a Which place card, then fills a Worth card with the place value three ways, as a count, a fraction and a decimal. An empty place inside the number holds a grey 0 labelled Place holder. On the third phase a Two places panel subtracts the worths of one digit in two columns, the difference in green. On the last phase a nudge arrow over each column adds or takes away one of that place and only that tile changes. A number pad. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of tiles on the chart. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Drag each digit to its column. Tap a digit. Say which place it is in, then how much it is worth.
